40c94f9b29:132b72ffa2674c2c.title: The Fusion of Commercial Civilization
40c94f9b29:132b72ffa2674c2c.summary: In his new book The Civilization of Commerce ( Encounter Books, October 2026 ), American Institute for Economic Research president Samuel Gregg explores the requirements, benefits, and positive features of a commercial society, which isn’t merely trading and exchanging goods but a civilization of growth in knowledge, specialization, networks, and institutions that is built on tradition, virtue, and law. Moving beyond the usual arguments for free markets, Gregg doesn’t base his case on personal liberty, economic growth, efficiency, and technological sophistication. While these elements are present, Gregg grounds his case in the virtues, traditions, institutions, habits, and mindset of a commercial civilization. The book draws on the case made by Friedrich Hayek and Adam Smith for what they both called “the Great Society.” This commercial society is built on a certain approach to knowledge, dynamism, institutions, and virtue that drives individual and social improvement, all of which contributes to opulence, defined by Smith as “overcoming deprivation.” Such a trajectory also requires a steady adherence to, and a continued building of social and moral capital that no one rationally designed, but that many in the past and present have contributed to and shaped. In this argument, we can trace Hayek’s beliefs and his views as a central figure in the Austrian School of Economics , aspects of the American founding and the nineteenth-century republic, Tocqueville ’s musings on democratic society, and most significantly, the influence of the Scottish Enlightenment . Gregg observes that much of the case for understanding commercial civilization turns on what leading Scottish thinkers identified in their developing society in the eighteenth century: a new type of economic and social ordering that broke with a largely static and, in many cases, impoverished existence. He demonstrates how Friedrich Hayek and Adam Smith’s Great Society liberated people “from economic stagnation…

40c94f9b29:dab670eec04342c8.title: The Invisible Shackle: How Bureaucracy Stifles the Economy and Constrains Our Freedom
40c94f9b29:dab670eec04342c8.summary: For millions of entrepreneurs , the greatest barrier to generating wealth is no longer market competition but the relentless expansion of regulations and administrative procedures. While governance is ostensibly designed to ensure order, modern bureaucracy has morphed into a formidable “invisible shackle.” Rather than functioning as a neutral tool of oversight, excessive red tape treats a citizen’s inherent right to produce as a conditional concession granted by the state through endless, discretionary hurdles. The sixth edition of the Index of Bureaucracy 2026, developed at the Adam Smith Center for Economic Freedom at Florida International University, offers an empirical diagnosis of this administrative drain. Analyzing 27 countries—20 from Latin America and the Caribbean (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guyana, Honduras, Jamaica, Mexico, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay, and Venezuela), representing 94.4% of regional GDP, and 7 from Europe (France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom), accounting for 59% of Europe’s GDP—the study maps the complete administrative burden cycle across three milestones of the business life cycle: opening, running, and closing. The findings offer an unvarnished look at how bureaucratic overload distorts economies, punishes small businesses, and destroys productive potential. The Relevance of Measuring Bureaucracy Quantifying bureaucracy is not a mere academic exercise; it is an urgent economic necessity. Historically, administrative complexity has been treated as an unavoidable cost of doing business. However, scholarly frameworks from public choice theory, institutional and neo-institutional economics, and modern studies of governance show that government rules and procedures tend to expand because of political incentives, institutional fragmentation, and the tendency of legislators to answer every social…
