ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.title: An engine of (pay) growth? Productivity and wages in the UK auto industry
ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.author: Van Reenen, John
ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.summary: To what extent do identical workers in an industry benefit from productivity growth in the same industry? We study this question in the context of the UK auto industry which experienced a thirteen-fold increase in output per worker between 1980 and 2018. Over the same period, auto workers saw substantially stronger hourly wage growth than workers in other manufacturing industries. Controlling for unobserved worker heterogeneity, the auto wage premium over other manufacturing workers doubled from 8% in the 1980s to 17% in the 2010s, while the manufacturing premium over the rest of the economy remained roughly stable at 5%. Interpreted through the lens of a rent sharing model, we estimate that 63% of the increase in the raw firm-level auto wage premium can be accounted for by strong productivity growth. In contrast, differential bargaining power between auto workers cannot account for these changes.

ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.author: Xu, Yaling
ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.author: Asani Sarkar
ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations. In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.title: Beliefs Over Contracts
ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.author: Collin B. Raymond
ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.summary: We study how firms choose among incentive contracts and how accurately managers predict their effects. Using a survey of managerial beliefs and a large-scale field experiment, we randomly assign agents at the market level to several widely used, expenditure-equivalent incentive schemes. In the field, the best-performing contract increases agent output and firm revenue by over 20% relative to the status quo, despite being ranked lower by managers, whereas the worst-performing contract performs as predicted. Managers correctly identify underperforming contracts but systematically underestimate top- performing ones. We document the sources of performance di!erences—labor supply responses rather than selection or pricing and the determinants of managerial predictability: contract complexity and managerial hierarchy. Our results highlight the importance of contract design for firm performance and reveal systematic limits to managerial cognition in shaping incentives.

ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.title: Asymmetric Information in Wage Contracts: Experimental Evidence and Welfare Implications
ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.author: Daniel Herbst
ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.summary: Compared to self-employment or performance-based pay, fixed wages reduce earnings uncertainty but are prone to market distortions through moral hazard and adverse selection. Using a model of wage contracts under asymmetric information, I show that these distortions map to marginal treatment response functions in a marginal treatment effects (MTE) framework. I apply this framework to a field experiment in which data-entry workers choose between a randomized fixed wage and a piece rate. I find evidence of both moral hazard and adverse selection: Fixed wages reduce worker productivity by an estimated 8.74 percent relative to the mean. Meanwhile, a 10 percent increase in the wage offer attracts a marginal worker whose productivity is higher by 1.90 percent of the mean. Using semi-parametric MTE estimation, I calculate the welfare loss associated with asymmetric information and the marginal values of public funds (MVPFs) for policies aimed at recovering this loss. I find that a tax on piece rates can mitigate adverse selection into fixed wages, generating tax revenue at social costs as low as $0.88 per dollar.

ecbefe1924:ac5b1d4244cec881.title: Reliability of AI Agents: Rater Effects, Drift, and the Return to an Evaluation Program
ecbefe1924:ac5b1d4244cec881.author: Mark Esposito
ecbefe1924:ac5b1d4244cec881.summary: Firms increasingly evaluate deployed AI agents using repeated human ratings, yet observed score changes may reflect the measurement process as much as changes in the agent itself. Firms also rarely know how long an evaluation remains informative as deployed systems evolve. We study reliability as a latent state using 2, 611 rubric-scored production interviews from a deployed voice-and-video interviewing agent, overlapping human reviewers, the agent's change log, and support tickets. Reviewer severity varied substantially: two reviewers assessing the same batches differed by 0.79 standard deviations on the composite index, and a shift in reviewer composition flattened the raw trend. After adjusting for reviewer effects and smoothing batch-level estimates, evaluated reliability increased by 0.53 standard deviations from March to August 2026. Reliability also shifted materially across logged deploys. At the estimated rate of unaccounted movement, forecast uncertainty reaches the magnitude of the largest observed deploy contrast after about five weeks, although this horizon is imprecisely estimated and based on a small number of step-like changes. An independent operational outcome moved in the same direction: interview-related support tickets fell by about 10% per month relative to technical-issue tickets. These data do not identify a causal effect of evaluation on performance. Instead, they show that longitudinal AI evaluation requires three checks: comparability across raters, evidence currency under drift, and corroboration with consequential operational outcomes.

ecbefe1924:409a2dd6ca59a95d.title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
ecbefe1924:409a2dd6ca59a95d.author: Christopher T. Stanton
ecbefe1924:409a2dd6ca59a95d.summary: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development. We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions. We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs. This in turn makes general skill firm-specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.

ecbefe1924:f856f0eb7ab7cad2.title: Rating Multiple Agents with Career Concerns
ecbefe1924:f856f0eb7ab7cad2.author: Huseyin Yildirim
ecbefe1924:f856f0eb7ab7cad2.summary: A principal designs ratings for multiple career-concerned agents with correlated talents, mapping outputs into arbitrary finite-variance statistics. Peer output both benchmarks effort and signals talent, making full disclosure suboptimal under confidential ratings. Relaxing Bayes plausibility to linear orthogonality yields a closed-form rating and computable effort bounds for general priors; under normality, the relaxation is exact. Optimal confidential ratings combine the full-disclosure wage with the Fisher score for effort: they are relative-performance when individual output is informative about talent and team-based when it is noisy. Public ratings must satisfy joint Bayes plausibility, weakening incentives; hence, the principal prefers confidential ratings, whereas agents prefer public ratings. A spectral decomposition characterizes public ratings under normality: small cost heterogeneity implies full disclosure regardless of the noise structure, whereas large cost heterogeneity or strong effort spillovers can induce partial disclosure to reallocate incentives. The results bear on performance ratings and pay transparency.

ecbefe1924:37b37d42031cfba7.title: Do weekend workers like their jobs?
ecbefe1924:37b37d42031cfba7.author: Mark Wooden
ecbefe1924:37b37d42031cfba7.summary: Weekend work is a pervasive feature of labor markets that comes with both potential benefits (e.g., higher pay, flexible schedules) and drawbacks (e.g., less social time). Nevertheless, robust evidence on weekend workers’ job satisfaction is lacking. Longitudinal data from 21 waves of the annual Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey (n=211, 077; i=26, 273) are used to estimate the association between weekend work and several dimensions of job satisfaction. Estimates from fixed effects models reveal that weekend work is associated with significantly lower levels of satisfaction with working hours and flexibility, but this does not translate into lower levels of overall job satisfaction. Additional analyses were conducted to test whether results varied with employment status, occupation and parental status. In general, the main finding applied to all groups examined. There were, however, marked differences across sub-groups in satisfaction with other job domains. Overall, the results suggest that, for most workers, the benefits of working weekends offset its disadvantages.

ecbefe1924:0c76a1df3fb235f8.title: Remote Work from the Office
ecbefe1924:0c76a1df3fb235f8.author: Emma Harrington
ecbefe1924:0c76a1df3fb235f8.summary: Roughly half of in-office days are spent entirely on Zoom calls or doing solo work according to a new survey of college-educated Americans. These workers commute in just to work remotely from the office. Existing measures of remote work that focus solely on working from home miss up to three quarters of its true prevalence. We use a collage of data to unpack the drivers of working remotely from the office. The biggest driver is geographic distance, which causes teammates to work in different offices or fully remotely. Other contributors include non-compliance with in-office policies, poor coordination on in-office days, and a tendency to take Zoom calls rather than booking meeting rooms even when everyone is in the office.

ecbefe1924:620ea2fd44250f2f.title: Training Your Replacement: Worker Incentives and the Pace of Automation
ecbefe1924:620ea2fd44250f2f.author: Peter Landry
ecbefe1924:620ea2fd44250f2f.summary: Firms ask workers to train AI systems that will replace them. We model this with a worker who can shirk, cooperate with training, or obstruct training while maintaining productivity. Because training ends the job but only cooperation completes training, dismissal becomes a weaker penalty for shirking. The firm must raise the worker’s rent, and the worker gains from their replacement. AI can create jobs paying more than they produce and eliminate jobs it never automates. Firms paying only wages may slow training. A credible completion bonus equal to the worker’s rent without AI removes both the gain and the slowdown.

ecbefe1924:46524f1965373964.title: The Occupational Ladder: Implications for Life-Cycle Wage Dynamics
ecbefe1924:46524f1965373964.author: Guido Matias Cortes
ecbefe1924:46524f1965373964.summary: Some occupations pay higher wages than others, even conditional on worker characteristics, implying that occupations can be ranked on a ladder. We develop a simple decomposition to study the role this occupational ladder plays in average wage growth and in the fanning out of wages over the life cycle. We present three main findings. First, the distribution of employment shifts towards higher-paying occupations as workers gain experience. This contributes modestly to average life-cycle wage growth, with greatest impact in early career. Second, this upward movement in the occupational employment distribution is not accompanied by increasing dispersion; thus, the occupational ladder does not directly contribute to the fanning out of wages. Third, early-career workers who are well-positioned on the occupational ladder tend to earn wages far below the occupational average. However, by mid-career, workers’ relative wages within occupations (their positions on the job ladder) no longer depend on their occupation. This change in the covariance between individuals’ positions on the job and occupational ladders is a major contributor to the fanning out of wages over workers’ careers.

ecbefe1924:1c5ef94bd23acb99.title: Task Expansion with Generative AI: Experimental Evidence on Middle-Skilled, Early-Career Workers
ecbefe1924:1c5ef94bd23acb99.author: Tschoepe, Nele
ecbefe1924:1c5ef94bd23acb99.summary: Does generative artificial intelligence (AI) expand the set of tasks that middle-skilled, early-career workers can successfully perform? In a field experiment with 673 final-year IT apprentices at twelve German vocational schools, we randomly assign access to AI for completing occupation-specific tasks. To identify task expansion, we study tasks both within the apprenticeship curriculum and deliberately beyond it. AI raises productivity substantially across all task types, with gains tending to be larger on tasks where performance without AI is lowest. Crucially, productivity increases by 26â€“31 percentage points on tasks beyond apprenticesâ€™ formal training, providing direct evidence of AI-enabled task expansion. These productivity gains do not come at the cost of reduced immediate task comprehension. Treatment effects are generally larger among apprentices with above-median AI literacy.

ecbefe1924:8cf67b22b6800fad.title: More than just Plug and Play: Early Evidence on Organisational Capital and AI Adoption
ecbefe1924:8cf67b22b6800fad.author: Riley, Rebecca
ecbefe1924:8cf67b22b6800fad.summary: This paper provides early evidence that AI adoption by firms is linked to management practices in unique ways. Using panel data from the UK Management and Expectations Survey (MES), we find that firms with higher baseline management scores are significantly more likely to adopt AI. This relationship is specific to AI: the same management practices show no relationship with the adoption of other technologies such as robotics, specialized equipment, or specialized software. We also find that management capabilities related to performance measurement appear strongly related to AI adoption. These results suggest that organisational complementarities are specific to different technologies, with implications for policies to encourage AI adoption by firms.

b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.title: Transforming Textile Waste into Circular Value: Innovation, Community Participation and Sustainable Entrepreneurship in Micro and Small Enterprises
b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.author: Sweta Patnaik
b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.summary: In an era marked by economic uncertainty and environmental urgency, entrepreneurs are increasingly turning to sustainable innovation as a pathway to resilience and growth. This paper examines how the transformation of textile off-cut waste into functional and marketable products serves as both an entrepreneurial response to material scarcity and a strategic contribution to the circular economy. In contrast to high-capital technological innovation, this form of resource-based creativity offers accessible, low-cost solutions for emerging enterprises, particularly in the fashion and textile sectors. Drawing on examples of micro and small businesses navigating uncertain economic terrain, the study highlights how such innovations can generate value, reduce waste, and meet growing consumer demand for sustainability. While many entrepreneurs falter in the face of early challenges, those who reframe problems as opportunities particularly through material reuse are better positioned to survive and scale. This paper argues that innovation rooted in environmental consciousness and adaptability is not only viable during times of uncertainty but essential for long-term entrepreneurial success and inclusive economic recovery.

b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.title: Current state and development prospects of franchising in the Republic of Uzbekistan: From an emerging market to a systemic driver of economic growth
b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.author: Malika Azimova
b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.summary: This article examines the institutional and economic conditions shaping the development of franchising in the Republic of Uzbekistan. Drawing on an analy-sis of the legal and regulatory framework, industry statistics, field research, and comparisons with selected international markets, the study identifies the main fac-tors limiting the sector's growth and proposes a phased model for its institutional development. Particular attention is given to regional disparities, the sectoral composition of the market, and the potential of locally developed franchise sys-tems to support entrepreneurship and expand employment opportunities. The empirical evidence covers the period 2024?2025 and includes an analysis of commercial concession agreements as well as expert interviews with market par-ticipants from eight regions of Uzbekistan.

b3ea4f41ab:82a934767f3d67c7.title: Sorting into entrepreneurial teams
b3ea4f41ab:82a934767f3d67c7.author: Marta Morazzoni
b3ea4f41ab:82a934767f3d67c7.summary: This paper studies how entrepreneurs sort into founding teams and how team composition shapes the firm distribution. We develop a theory of career choice and team formation in which skill complementarities make team entrepreneurship attractive for agents with unbalanced skill profiles, while talent similarity makes teaming preferable to other career options. Using matched employer-employee and balance-sheet data from Portugal, we show that teams combining similar talent with diverse specializations create larger, more productive, and longer-lived firms; yet founders with dissimilar skills are less likely to start firms together. We calibrate the model to reproduce these patterns and use it to quantify the cost of imperfect founder matching. Counterfactuals show that reducing founders’ biased exposure reallocates activity from low-productivity solo firms toward more productive teams. An optimal-assignment benchmark reveals that even unbiased random search leaves substantial gains unrealized because high-surplus matches fail to form.

b3ea4f41ab:daeafea108d23544.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
b3ea4f41ab:daeafea108d23544.author: Asani Sarkar
b3ea4f41ab:daeafea108d23544.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations. In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

b3ea4f41ab:6735834859328ccf.title: Breaking into Supply Chains : Experimental Evidence on Procurement Training for Women-Owned SMEs
b3ea4f41ab:6735834859328ccf.author: Neelamraju, Kalyan N.
b3ea4f41ab:6735834859328ccf.summary: Women-owned-or-led small and medium-sized enterprises (WSMEs) are underrepresented in public and corporate supply chains worldwide. There is growing interest in promoting SMEs’ and WSMEs’ integration into value chains, but limited causal evidence whether interventions to support their participation in procurement are effective. This paper conducts a phased randomized controlled trial to estimate the impacts of corporate procurement training for WSMEs in Colombia. The program increases procurement knowledge and readiness, resulting in a ten percentage point increase in registrations to corporate portals, and an eight percentage point increase in the likelihood of submitting a bid. Impacts on winning bids are concentrated in WSMEs with prior procurement knowledge or experience, whose probability of winning a contract increases by eight to nine percentage points. These impacts are approximately twenty percent of the control means. More broadly, the paper illustrates how complier-weighted treatment effects can be used to evaluate programs delivered through a funnel-shaped participation process, common in private sector development interventions.

b3ea4f41ab:331a019c46c049c4.title: Do public transfers crowd out the effects of remittances? Social protection, and entrepreneurship in eight communities in West-Africa
b3ea4f41ab:331a019c46c049c4.author: Jessica Hagen-Zanker
b3ea4f41ab:331a019c46c049c4.summary: Remittances and social protection programmes have become two of the most important sources of financial support for households across low- and middle-income countries. While both have been linked to household investment and livelihood diversification, little is known about how they jointly influence entrepreneurship. This paper examines whether public transfers, in the form of cash transfers and school feeding support, crowd out or in household entrepreneurship and whether private transfers, in the form of remittances, complement or substitute for public transfers in shaping entrepreneurship. Using household survey data from eight communities in West Africa, we analyse the relationship between social protection, remittances and a range of entrepreneurial outcomes. The results provide little evidence that social protection systematically influences household entrepreneurship or alters the relationship between remittances and business activity. In contrast, remittances remain consistently associated with business creation and entrepreneurial intentions across multiple contexts. These findings suggest that expanding social protection does not diminish the productive role of remittances and highlight the importance of considering public and private sources of household support jointly when assessing policies aimed at promoting entrepreneurship and inclusive economic development.

b3ea4f41ab:5c51b890307caeaa.title: No Women No Innovation? The Effect of Women on Boards on Hard and Soft Innovation in SMEs
b3ea4f41ab:5c51b890307caeaa.author: Giulio Ferrigno
b3ea4f41ab:5c51b890307caeaa.summary: The role of women on corporate boards and its impact on innovation remains heavily debated. While existing literature offers conflicting perspectives on whether female board representation spurs or hinders innovaiton, most research has focused exlusively on large firms. This studt adresses this gap by investigating the causal impact of women on boards on both "hard" (technological) and "soft" (non-technological) innovation within SMEs. Using a longitudinal dataset f 2762 Italian innovative SMEs from 2015 to 2024 and a 2SLS identification strategy, we find highly nuanced patterns. For hard innovation, the instrumented model reveals a robust positive causal impacr, reversing a negative baseline coefficient and exposing a severe negative selection bias. For soft innovation, a stable positive impact is confirmed. Our findings provide crucial causal evidence for SMEs' governance, while offering tailored insights for policymakers and practitioners to incentivize women' management roles in SMES.

b3ea4f41ab:ba33fe9d21357b95.title: Taxing Entrepreneurial Wealth: Evidence from Norway, 2021–2025
b3ea4f41ab:ba33fe9d21357b95.author: Marius A. K. Ring
b3ea4f41ab:ba33fe9d21357b95.summary: Whether imposing higher taxes on business owners adversely affects business activity by constraining investment and inducing capitalist flight is a central question in the ongoing debate on how to tax the ultra wealthy. To shed new light, I exploit a series of related Norwegian reforms during 2021–2024 that increased dividend tax rates, removed migration-related capital gains tax loopholes, and nearly doubled the effective marginal tax rate on business wealth. These reforms spurred international debate and, allegedly, an “exodus” of Norwegian billionaires (Financial Times, 2023). While I document clear effects on migration, these responses are concentrated among the top 0.1% of the wealth distribution and mostly confined to 2022 and 2023. My results indicate that at most 100 individuals left due to the reforms. I find no evidence of significant outmigration or reduced inflows of startup founders or inventors. I estimate that absent any outmigration, wealth tax revenues would have increased by 75% from 2021 to 2024. Reform-driven outmigration lowers the revenue gain to 71.5%. My findings further show that outmigrating owners’ firms remain economically active and do not reduce investment. In a broader set of analyses, I examine whether business outcomes are affected, regardless of whether owners outmigrate, since firms may reduce investment both due to liquidity constraints or distortions to owners’ savings decisions. I compare firms owned by Norwegian individuals subject to the wealth tax with firms owned by foreigners and other tax-exempt entities. By merging historical ownership data from Orbis with the Norwegian shareholder register, I perform these analyses on both Norwegian and foreign-domiciled firms. Across settings, I find no evidence that Norwegian-owned firms pay out more dividends or invest less after the reforms, nor is there any evidence that the reform induced more bankruptcies. These findings indicate that the short-run economic costs of wealth…

b3ea4f41ab:751df8fd01634f75.title: Capital for growth: the evolution, structure and role of private equity and venture capital in Italy
b3ea4f41ab:751df8fd01634f75.author: Pietro Tramontano
b3ea4f41ab:751df8fd01634f75.summary: This paper analyses the Italian private equity and venture capital market. Although total investment more than doubled between 2015 and 2025, the Italian market remains less developed than those of the other main European economies. Private equity investment is strongly oriented towards technology- and knowledge-intensive sectors, with significant participation by foreign funds. The public sector plays a prominent role in fundraising by Italian operators, whereas the contribution of private institutional investors remains relatively limited. Compared with firms in the same sector, size class and geographical area, private equity target firms are larger, more profitable and better capitalized; after turning to private equity, they record faster growth in total assets, employment, and investment, particularly in intangible assets. The further development of private capital markets in Italy could be fostered by a greater involvement of private investors and a wider availability of patient capital to support firms' growth and innovation.

b3ea4f41ab:c21f2ccd36cda662.title: Who Replaces Spirit? Entry, Exit, and Low-End Fares
b3ea4f41ab:c21f2ccd36cda662.author: E. Mina Guler
b3ea4f41ab:c21f2ccd36cda662.summary: A federal court blocked JetBlue’s acquisition of Spirit Airlines in January 2024 to protect consumers who relied on Spirit’s low fares. Spirit failed anyway and ceased operations in May 2026. We ask whether the prohibition protected consumers. Using DB1B data for 2022–2025, we estimate the effect of Spirit’s exit across the 1, 427 routes it served. The 5th and 10th percentile fares rise by 8.6 and 5.8 log points; mean and median fares are unaffected. Where a carrier entered, the bottom is unaffected and mean fares fall. Theharm comes from exit without replacement, which entry policy does not reach.

b3ea4f41ab:c0e0e32788fe8d73.title: Global Entrepreneurial Talent Flows: Widely Funded, Selectively Successful?
b3ea4f41ab:c0e0e32788fe8d73.author: Henry Woo
b3ea4f41ab:c0e0e32788fe8d73.summary: Immigrant founders of US venture-backed startups exit successfully more often than native founders. Does this hold worldwide? Using career histories for 913, 226 founder-firm pairs in 213 countries (1990–2026), we compare founders who build abroad (expats) or return home after foreign experience (returnees) with comparable local founders in the same country. Both expats and returnees raise early funding more often globally. Expats' success premium, however, concentrates in the US (18 percent) and UK (26 percent), especially among those entering the US through graduate school, work, or direct founding. Returnees rarely show such a premium. Capital follows mobile founders across borders, but success follows them selectively.

b3ea4f41ab:00f4ff9749ca8087.title: Self-Employment and Regional Development in Disruptive Times - Germany 1895 - 2020
b3ea4f41ab:00f4ff9749ca8087.author: Michael Wyrwich
b3ea4f41ab:00f4ff9749ca8087.summary: We examine the long-term relationship between historical levels of self-employment and economic performance in different regions of Germany. A particular distinction is made between West Germany and the eastern part of the country, that came after WWII for forty years under socialist regime. Regional self-employment rates exhibit high correlation over time periods exceeding a century. In West Germany, high and increasing levels of self-employment are significantly associated with high current levels of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per population, despite several major historical shocks. That such a relationship cannot be found in East Germany could be a legacy of the socialist period where the government performed anti-entrepreneurial policies. We also find a positive relationship between historical self-employment and patenting in both parts of the country. This relationship is, however, somewhat weaker in East Germany, which experienced considerably more historical shocks than West Germany.

b3ea4f41ab:d38ee65572d7e3dc.title: Regional Dynamics of Innovation in Europe 2000-2020 A Tale of Convergence, Persistence, and the Illusion of Catch-Up
b3ea4f41ab:d38ee65572d7e3dc.author: Michael Wyrwich
b3ea4f41ab:d38ee65572d7e3dc.summary: This study examines the dynamics of regional innovation activity in Europe from 2000 to 2020 using patent applications. Standard convergence measures indicate that regional disparities are narrowing, with initially lagging regions catching up to the leading ones. Our analysis reveals two persistent â€˜clubsâ€™: the â€˜laggingâ€™ and the â€˜advancedâ€™ regions. Although these groups are becoming increasingly similar, the differences between them remain largely unchanged. Despite two decades of growth, the disparity between the two clubs still accounts for a great deal of the total variation in regional patenting. These patterns suggest a convergence illusion that is overlooked in the current scholarly debate.

b3ea4f41ab:8aa7edf1245c180a.title: Exploring Chilean student perceptions of Opportunity entrepreneurship?
b3ea4f41ab:8aa7edf1245c180a.author: Muraro, Vinicius
b3ea4f41ab:8aa7edf1245c180a.summary: This study explores how Chilean university students perceive entrepreneurship, exploring whether they see it as an opportunity to address societal challenges or primarily as an enterprise creation. The research focuses on how these perceptions vary by gender in front of sociodemographic, academic, and institutional influential factors. Using a quantitative approach, we collected data from a sample of 973 students from different fields of study and conducted statistical analyses to determine the importance of factors that determine entrepreneurial attitudes. The results reveal that the majority of students see entrepreneurship as an opportunity to influence society and address social issues. Sociodemographic factors do not show statistical significance, suggesting that, within this specific population, they do not substantially alter the motivations for entrepreneurship. Although students may share similar views on the opportunity or business nature of entrepreneurship, the factors shaping this perception differ by gender. Among these factors, the value of active and engaged university support, especially in the form of experiential learning methodologies, in fostering opportunitydriven entrepreneurship is highlighted. In contrast, resources such as infrastructure and institutional culture, while important, appear to play a more limited role. This research underscores the need for a holistic approach to entrepreneurship education, but with special attention to particular differences between the segments being served, integrating institutional support with hands-on learning methods to better cultivate an entrepreneurial culture to economic growth and mindset geared towards addressing societal problems.

abdecb2e4b:24ab7c4bab435169.title: Interlinking National Fast Payment Systems
abdecb2e4b:24ab7c4bab435169.author: Lee Reiners
abdecb2e4b:24ab7c4bab435169.summary: International payments are often relatively slow and expensive, especially if not denominated in the major currencies. These costs serve as effectively a tax on remittances home from expatriate workers from poor countries, and on cross-border retail purchases from poor countries. 18d1edb9f2:08227758a80d9e92.title: Arenas of Change: Towards sustainable material flows
18d1edb9f2:08227758a80d9e92.author: Stihl, Linda
18d1edb9f2:08227758a80d9e92.summary: The sustainability imperative calls for a sharp reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and virgin materials use. This requires the transformation of currently unsustainable global and linear value chains (GVCs) to regenerative and circular supply chains (CSCs). To deal with the complexities of such a shift, this paper suggests Arenas of Change as a theoretical perspective and methodological approach, capturing interaction spaces of actors who engage in changing how goods are produced, distributed and consumed, and how waste is recovered and reduced. Actors are conceptualised as being embedded in multi-scalar network, institutional and governance structures, which can enable or hinder change processes. We argue that the possibility of Arenas of Change to effectuate and accelerate shifts from GVCs towards CSCs depends on the realisation of synergies in four domains: i) business logics, models, and innovation; ii) consumption and user practices, iii) modes of governance, and iv) policies and discourses. Arenas of Change are thus a prism through which the interdependencies between domains, multiple scales and levels, and actors' strategies can be analysed. Thereby, Arenas of Change can contribute to theory-building about transformations from global and linear to regenerative and circular supply chains, and conditions that enable, accelerate or hinder such systemic change. Furthermore, by enhancing analytical leverage to comprehensively capture the complexity of such transformations, we propose Arenas of Change as an approach to design impactful interventions, and to evaluate their effects.

18d1edb9f2:1858feb61cdf0f32.title: Ideas and Firm Dynamics When It Takes Two to Tango
18d1edb9f2:1858feb61cdf0f32.author: Honghao Wang
18d1edb9f2:1858feb61cdf0f32.summary: Teams of inventors now produce over 80 percent of U.S. patents, up from just 45 percent in 1976. Over the same period, inventor employment has become increasingly concentrated in large firms, rising six times more than overall employment concentration. To explain these trends, we develop a new model of endogenous team formation within firms and embed it in a general equilibrium model of the inventor labor market. Teams increase firms’ returns to scale by increasing the likelihood of productive matches between inventors. The value of these matches rises over time, possibly driven by increasing knowledge specialization. This causes large firms to expand and small firms to shrink in equilibrium, accounting for the observed increase in inventor employment concentration. Because firms do not internalize knowledge spillovers, there is misallocation of inventors across firms. The rise of team production amplifies this misallocation by a factor of six by reallocating inventors away from small firms that generate disproportionately large knowledge spillovers.

18d1edb9f2:15693bc5b1222e10.title: Risk and Reward in Science Funding: A Field Experiment on Grant Evaluation
18d1edb9f2:15693bc5b1222e10.author: Christoph Grimpe
18d1edb9f2:15693bc5b1222e10.summary: Public money for research is distributed through peer-review but it has been criticized to disfavour risky science. Traditional review typically asks reviewers to compress multiple dimensions such as novelty, feasibility, impact, etc. into a single overall score, and this compression may penalise proposals whose potential is high but uncertain. The subjective expected utility (SEU) framework instead asks them to assess separately the utility and likelihood of a proposal's potential outcomes without issuing an overall compressed score. This paper examines whether structuring peer review in this way, systematically alters the ranking of grant proposals. Using a field experiment embedded in a real funding call, we have the same proposals evaluated under either traditional criteria or SEU criteria, with a treatment assignment that we argue to be as good as random. We find that the two methods produce very different orderings of the same applications: their percentile ranks are essentially uncorrelated, and individual applications shift considerably in relative position. SEU reorders applications along dimensions traditional review leaves implicit: 'High-Likelihood High-Utility' applications are ranked higher and 'Low-Likelihood Low-Utility' applications lower under SEU as compared to traditional review. Importantly, we do not observe a significant up- ranking of ‘Low-Likelihood High-Utility’ applications under SEU relative to the traditional review. On the contrary, 'High-Likelihood Low-Utility' application show a significant yet modest down-ranking under SEU relative to traditional review. These ranking differences translate into substantially different funding outcomes. Applying the funding cutoff that corresponds to the number of applications actually funded to each ranking, the 3 applications that would be funded under SEU were, without exception, those that referees had classified as high-likelihood (23 'High-Likelihood High-Utility' and 2 'High-Likelihood…

18d1edb9f2:425f35c08608d92e.title: Patents, Pay and People: How Innovation Reshapes the Workforce
18d1edb9f2:425f35c08608d92e.author: Taymaz, Erol
18d1edb9f2:425f35c08608d92e.summary: We examine how innovation shapes firm-level workforce dynamics using rich administrative data from Turkiye, a developing economy characterized by medium-technology, incremental innovation. We find that patent-based innovation increases both firm size and average daily wages, with the largest employment gains among workers earning just above the median wage. To uncover the mechanisms behind these outcomes, we construct worker transition matrices. Relative to comparable non-innovative firms, innovative firms (i) retain incumbent workers at higher rates, particularly at the top of the wage distribution, (ii) promote retained workers into higher wage bins more frequently, and (iii) hire more new workers, disproportionately into higher wage bins. Finally, occupational composition analysis shows that employment growth is concentrated among technical and production occupations, consistent with the medium-technology, incremental nature of innovation in our sample.

18d1edb9f2:7117c119118e8d29.title: Scientific isolation? The consequences of Trump's China initiative on Chinese research
18d1edb9f2:7117c119118e8d29.author: Westin, Karolina
18d1edb9f2:7117c119118e8d29.summary: The 2018 China Initiative by the Trump administration complicated procedures and reduced funding for U.S.-China research collaborations. Using Scopus data, we analyze its impact on Chinese research. We find that it significantly lowered the quality of both publications and co-authors of Chinese researchers with prior U.S. collaborations compared to those with prior European collaborations, and reduced yearly citations for affected researchers by 6%. The effect was stronger for high-productivity Chinese researchers in U.S.-dominated fields. While China is at the forefront of the scientific frontier, it still depends more on the U.S. than the reverse.

fd826003ba:97d3780fdbff4a98.title: Episode 108: Tom Schwantje on Choosing Middle Managers and Delegating Power in Multi-Ethnic Countries
fd826003ba:97d3780fdbff4a98.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:97d3780fdbff4a98.summary: Organisations face a trade-off when appointing and delegating power to middle managers. On the one hand, the manager may take decisions that are not beneficial to the organisation. On the other hand, the manager may have better local information. In multi-ethnic countries this trade-off shapes whether the organisation may want to appoint a manager co-ethnic to the market served or co-ethnic to the organisation itself. This is studied in the context of Ethiopia, where an unexpected civil war increased the salience of ethnicity.

fd826003ba:10eb88327ee6e17c.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:10eb88327ee6e17c.summary: This paper studies the effect of managers for the performance of public hospitals, specifically following a reform in Chile that changed their recruitment process. The main findings are that the reform decreased mortality, likely through the mechanism of improving the quality of managers (e.g., replacing managers without management degrees with managers with management degrees).

fd826003ba:6efc59758fb1d8a7.title: Episode 106: Alexia Delfino and Miguel Espinosa on Value Dissonance at Work
fd826003ba:6efc59758fb1d8a7.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:6efc59758fb1d8a7.summary: This paper studies what happens when a worker has a different set of values than (a) their boss, or (b) their colleagues. Productivity is lower workers with such value dissonance, and the mechanism appears to be worse worker morale and worse communication between worker and manager.

fd826003ba:9e3018f394a3b4a7.title: Episode 105: Michael Frakes on Doctor Diversity and Racial Health Differences
fd826003ba:9e3018f394a3b4a7.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:9e3018f394a3b4a7.summary: This paper studies whether the racial diversity of medical providers (mostly doctors) in the hospital, affects the health outcomes of minority patients. There is a big effect and, most importantly, it does not only operate through the concordance between individual patient and individual doctor: having more diverse doctors in the hospital generates positive externalities that go beyond the patient-doctor relation.

fd826003ba:999aee89b4154734.title: Episode 104: Victoria Angelova on the Comparison between Algorithms and Humans Making Decisions
fd826003ba:999aee89b4154734.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:999aee89b4154734.summary: This paper studies whether human decision-makers can improve on algorithmic recommendations, in the setting of bail decisions in the criminal justice system. Bail judges receive recommendations from predictive algorithms and can choose to confirm or override them. The paper finds that most judges do not add value beyond the algorithm, although a minority do.

f3fd1ffa24:8c142c33b72c8379.title: The U.S. Oil Sector’s Role in Restraining Prices
f3fd1ffa24:8c142c33b72c8379.author: Thomas Klitgaard
f3fd1ffa24:8c142c33b72c8379.summary: The start of the Middle East conflict in early 2026 caused an unprecedented drop in global petroleum supply. In response, oil prices jumped—but not to unprecedentedly high levels. The U.S. oil sector was a key factor in moderating the shock. For one, its steady increases in drilling helped create a large oversupply in the global market before the conflict, making it less of a challenge to offset the drop in Middle East oil output. In addition, U.S. commercial and government inventories were rapidly drawn down, filling half the gap between global supply and demand in the second quarter by some estimates. Inventories, though, are a limited resource and U.S. stockpiles stopped falling in July. As a consequence, the continued shortfall in global production has been managed by running down inventories in the rest of the world.

f3fd1ffa24:f264753704ee9bc6.title: How Market Position Shapes Credit Card Interest Rates
f3fd1ffa24:f264753704ee9bc6.author: Kyle Herkenhoff and Juan M. Morelli
f3fd1ffa24:f264753704ee9bc6.summary: Why is it that two borrowers who look much alike can be offered very different rates when applying for a credit card? In a recent paper , we address this question by examining how the rate offered changes when the lender’s funding cost falls. Data on 14 million newly issued cards show that when a lender's funding costs decline, the lender passes less of that decline on to the offer rate when it holds a large market share. That is, two borrowers with similar credit scores and incomes borrowing from the same lender can see noticeably different interest rates on the credit card they are applying for.

f3fd1ffa24:c48a20582dc18d57.title: How Do Banking Supervisors Deal with Failing Banks?
f3fd1ffa24:c48a20582dc18d57.author: Sergio Correia, Stephan Luck, and Emil Verner
f3fd1ffa24:c48a20582dc18d57.summary: In this post, we discuss insights from a recent staff report on the role of banking supervision in identifying and disciplining failing banks. We show that bank failures typically result from supervisory closure decisions based on hard information about book equity. Yet hard information is itself partly produced by supervision, as our evidence suggests that supervisors require troubled banks to recognize potential losses. We argue that supervision faces a trade-off: Stricter supervision can reduce the costs of resolving failing banks, but it can also lead to tighter regulatory capital constraints and hold back credit supply.

f3fd1ffa24:a4402c9f2991db79.title: Evaluating New LinkedIn Labor Market Tightness Indicators
f3fd1ffa24:a4402c9f2991db79.summary: Measures of labor market tightness (LMT) describe how difficult it is for firms to find workers. The labor market is considered tight if there are few job seekers available relative to job openings, implying stronger wage pressures as employers compete for scarce job seekers. Thus, good measures of LMT are important for predicting wage inflation and calibrating monetary policy. Recently, the hiring platform LinkedIn began producing three innovative LMT measures based on its user data. In this post, we use public data from the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) to evaluate the ability of these novel measures to predict wage and price inflation relative to existing LMT measures, finding that one stands out as particularly useful and timely.

f3fd1ffa24:42008bb79cf11289.title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share?
f3fd1ffa24:42008bb79cf11289.summary: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output .

f3fd1ffa24:22a1cb8ad31be2ec.title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account?
f3fd1ffa24:22a1cb8ad31be2ec.author: Julian di Giovanni
f3fd1ffa24:22a1cb8ad31be2ec.summary: The AI boom is showing up in different corners of the U.S. economy, including international trade. Imports of semiconductors, servers, and computing equipment have climbed sharply yet the U.S. current account deficit has been largely unchanged. To better understand how the AI boom has not substantially affected the trade balance, consider that the current account is dictated by the gap between domestic saving and investment spending. It turns out that aggregate saving and investment spending have not changed much during the AI boom. Aggregate investment has not risen due to weakness outside the AI sector and business saving has remained robust.

f3fd1ffa24:45d0a3bff02d5db0.title: Prices, Prices, Prices: Overall Inflation and the Costs You Care About
f3fd1ffa24:45d0a3bff02d5db0.summary: As fall starts to show itself in cooler weather, I want to discuss a topic that usually raises temperatures: inflation. Like a budget-conscious consumer, the Federal Reserve is highly attuned to changes in the price of goods and services; minimizing such swings is one of the Fed’s primary duties, after all. But how does the Fed’s view of prices differ from that of a consumer? And how does the Fed go about stabilizing prices writ large when it lacks the ability to set prices directly? In this post, I explore that apparent paradox from the perspective of a central banker (though I remain a budget-conscious consumer when off duty).

f3fd1ffa24:2fd0334d84f65de0.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
f3fd1ffa24:2fd0334d84f65de0.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations . In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

f3fd1ffa24:00bc17cbb1a550c2.title: Firm Heterogeneity and the Response of Investment to Monetary Policy
f3fd1ffa24:00bc17cbb1a550c2.summary: It is well known that monetary policy affects firms’ investment decisions. But which firms are the most responsive to changes in interest rates? And does this responsiveness vary over time? The literature has given diverse answers to this question, focusing on characteristics such as firm size, age, and financial position, and mostly studying these traits in isolation. In this post based on a recent Staff Report , we explore how investment responsiveness to monetary policy changes across firms and over time. We find that investment by most firms in most time periods responds little to monetary policy. For some firms in some periods, however, investment is very responsive to changes in interest rates. While these instances of strong sensitivity correlate with several firm traits, there is substantial variation that cannot easily be linked to specific characteristics of firms. Our findings therefore underscore the importance of considering the entire distribution of investment responses rather than focusing on the average effect.

f3fd1ffa24:60233756dac81b20.title: How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices?
f3fd1ffa24:60233756dac81b20.author: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
f3fd1ffa24:60233756dac81b20.summary: There has been a lot of interest in how tariffs affect consumer prices (for example, Cavallo et al. 2021 , 2025 ). In this post, we present results from our new research paper that estimates the effects of the 2025-26 tariffs on retail consumer prices. We find that for every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer goods prices increase by about a quarter of a percent after one year. Roughly two-thirds of the effect arises because tariffs raise the prices of imported consumer goods. The remaining third arises indirectly: tariffs increase the prices of goods made in the U.S. because producers pay more for imported parts and materials, and because producers raise their markups when competing imports cost more. The effects differ in their timing. Prices of imported goods respond quickly to tariffs, while prices of U.S.-made goods adjust over six to twelve months as higher costs move through the supply chain.

f3fd1ffa24:91124a79f6cc5b49.title: Insured, but Still on the Hook: Who Bears the Most Risk in Homeowner’s Insurance?
f3fd1ffa24:91124a79f6cc5b49.summary: In an April post , using millions of homeowners' insurance contracts matched with property-level exposure and disaster risk, we showed that although households are insured, they are still "on the hook” because deductibles and coverage limits leave homeowners responsible for part of a loss. Because insurers cannot perfectly observe how well homeowners maintain or protect their properties (a problem known as “moral hazard”), contract terms such as deductibles can play an important role in balancing risk sharing and incentives. By requiring homeowners to bear part of a loss, insurers can preserve incentives for policyholders to take actions that reduce damage risk. In this post, we quantify the cost of keeping homeowners on the hook. How costly is moral hazard in homeowner's insurance? How much risk must households retain to preserve these incentives? And, importantly, who ultimately bears that residual risk? The short answer is that keeping homeowners on the hook costs insurers relatively little, but it leaves households with substantial risk, especially those least able to absorb a large loss.

f3fd1ffa24:023576dba8e34ff8.title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market
f3fd1ffa24:023576dba8e34ff8.summary: Geoeconomic risk—the risk that firms incur valuation losses when countries deploy economic, trade, or financial leverage for geopolitical aims—has become a first-order concern for investors. In this post, based on our recent Staff Report , we document that domestic U.S. stocks expose investors to substantial geoeconomic risk through firms' global supply-chain relationships, affecting investors' returns and portfolio allocation. We also find that investors are compensated for bearing geoeconomic risk through higher risk premia.

f3fd1ffa24:fe7f8ea660814215.title: The Role of Repos in Monetary Policy Implementation
f3fd1ffa24:fe7f8ea660814215.author: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
f3fd1ffa24:fe7f8ea660814215.summary: In the first two posts of this three-part series, we discussed private market participants that are active in repo markets for profit-making motives. Central banks are also active repo market participants, but their reasons often differ from those of private participants. In today’s post, we discuss how central banks use repos to manage liquidity in the financial system and implement monetary policy.

f3fd1ffa24:c9eae9bec5af78cb.title: Follow the Cash! Microstructure of Repo Markets
f3fd1ffa24:c9eae9bec5af78cb.author: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
f3fd1ffa24:c9eae9bec5af78cb.summary: The repo market in the U.S. is a mosaic of segments with distinct participants and various settlement and clearing practices. Why do large cash lenders typically settle their trades through a third-party agent? Why does the interdealer market clear through a central counterparty? Why do levered investors favor bilateral trades? In the second post of this series, we follow the cash as it navigates through repo markets to better understand the costs and benefits that shape the existing market structures.

f3fd1ffa24:5ccfa8b9d29f8a21.title: Who’s Borrowing and Lending in Repo Markets?
f3fd1ffa24:5ccfa8b9d29f8a21.author: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
f3fd1ffa24:5ccfa8b9d29f8a21.summary: Repo markets play a vital role in the U.S. financial system. In this three-part series, we examine who participates in these markets, what trade-offs influence how different repo segments are structured, and why repos matter for monetary policy. Today's post introduces repo transactions, focusing on the major private-sector participants and why they engage in these markets.

91cd3b3295:85b9892d1c6fbdb2.title: Are Nonprofit Tax Exemptions and Deductions "Federal Financial Assistance"? Should They Be?
91cd3b3295:85b9892d1c6fbdb2.author: Lloyd Hitoshi Mayer
91cd3b3295:85b9892d1c6fbdb2.summary: Two recent federal court decisions have reignited the debate over whether “Federal financial assistance” as used in four federal anti-discrimination statutes includes the tax benefits enjoyed by most nonprofit organizations. Both courts concluded that it does. While an appellate court reversed one decision, and the other case settled without appellate review, these holdings create significant uncertainty. And this uncertainty affects the more than 1.8 million tax-exempt nonprofits, many if not most of which do not receive federal financial assistance through other channels and so could safely conclude these statutes do not reach them, absent these decisions. This uncertainty is also magnified by recent Trump administration assertions that nonprofits and other private entities receiving federal financial assistance must conform to that administration’s views of what constitutes illegal discrimination. This Article first considers whether the two recent decisions were correct in deciding that federal financial assistance in this context includes nonprofit tax benefits and determines that the weight of authority strongly supports the conclusion that they were not. More specifically, it reviews the relevant statutory language, existing regulatory and other administrative guidance, and court decisions and commentary addressing this issue to reach the conclusion that “Federal financial assistance” as used in Title VI, Title IX, the Rehabilitation Act and the Age Discrimination Act does not include the exemption from federal income tax enjoyed by most nonprofits and, for charities, the eligibility to receive tax-deductible contributions. This Article also considers the contrary arguments asserted by courts and commentators and explains why none of those arguments are persuasive. This conclusion does not end the matter, however, as those same arguments suggest that Congress should expand the reach of these anti-discrimination statutes to include nonprofits that enjoy…

91cd3b3295:4a6f4c3df37c1c37.title: Redemption! Valuing Closely Held Companies After Connelly
91cd3b3295:4a6f4c3df37c1c37.author: Adam Chodorow
91cd3b3295:4a6f4c3df37c1c37.summary: In Connelly v. United States , the Supreme Court resolved a long-standing dispute over how to treat redemption obligations when valuing a decedent’s shares in a closely held company. The Court held that redemption obligations do not offset corporate-owned life insurance proceeds obtained to fund a redemption, upsetting a long-standing practice. While the Court undoubtedly reached the right conclusion, it (1) failed to address important arguments the parties and amici raised; (2) assumed away the effects of discounts, premiums and different valuation techniques, which would have complicated the analysis without changing the conclusion; and (3) muddied the water somewhat by leaving open the possibility of a different outcome where companies use operating assets to fund a redemption. This Article lays out the various authorities that bear on this question, sets forth additional grounds supporting the Court’s conclusion, including the arguments the Court sidestepped, addresses the complexities avoided by using a simple hypothetical and explains why the reasoning applies equally to situations where operating assets are used to fund a redemption. Finally, the Article identifies different ways taxpayers can use insurance to fund redemptions while avoiding the results in Connelly .

91cd3b3295:773fe8a2e2df3085.title: State Tax Discrimination and Internal Consistency
91cd3b3295:773fe8a2e2df3085.author: Michael T. Fatale
91cd3b3295:773fe8a2e2df3085.summary: The contours of the U.S. Supreme Court’s dormant Commerce Clause doctrine of internal consistency, which asks whether a state tax intrinsically overreaches in imposing a burden upon interstate commerce, are difficult to understand. This is despite the fact that a determination that a state tax violates internal consistency can have significant state fiscal consequences. This uncertainty was suggested again by the recent case, Zilka v. Tax Review Board City of Philadelphia , for which the Supreme Court later denied certiorari. See 304 A.3d 1153 (Pa. 2023), cert. denied , 145 S. Ct. 1045 (2025). The parameters of the internal consistency doctrine should not be so obscure. The doctrine would be more logical and understandable if it were primarily utilized, not as a stand-alone test, but as a tool to evaluate state tax discrimination, i.e., whether a state has impermissibly sought to favor local businesses over businesses based in other states. This Article explains how this approach would be more firmly grounded in the Court’s current approach to the dormant Commerce Clause and, for example, would be consistent with the Court’s “undue burden” balancing inquiry as recently reconsidered in National Pork Producers Council v. Ross , 143 S. Ct. 1142 (2023). This Article also sets forth how this analysis would comport with the Supreme Court’s prior internal consistency cases, including Comptroller of the Treasury of Maryland v. Wynne , 575 U.S. 542 (2015), and recent state court cases applying the internal consistency test.

91cd3b3295:76817f675a4a9bf5.title: The Mother of All Tax Shelters
91cd3b3295:76817f675a4a9bf5.author: Michael Doran
91cd3b3295:76817f675a4a9bf5.summary: By its own account, the federal government spends more than $500 billion every year to subsidize retirement savings in 401(k) plans, IRAs and similar arrangements. That figure is larger than the annual budget of every government agency other than the four largest. The theory behind this massive subsidy is that it gives workers at all income levels an incentive to save money that they would otherwise spend, thereby enhancing retirement security, reducing old-age poverty and easing dependence on Social Security. But the theory is wrong. The retirement tax subsidy is anything but egalitarian. Less than five percent of the subsidy goes to households in the bottom 40 percent of the income distribution scale, and more than 60 percent goes to households in the top 20 percent. And among higher-income households, the subsidy generally does not encourage saving. Instead, the affluent respond to the subsidy primarily by moving assets from taxable investment accounts to tax-exempt retirement accounts. In short, the federal government spends more than half a trillion dollars every year to provide windfalls to higher-income households with little meaningful increase in retirement security for lower-income and middle-income households. It is time to acknowledge that the retirement tax subsidy is a tax shelter, nothing more and nothing less, and to reset tax policy accordingly.

91cd3b3295:ab26e9eb371960ca.title: The Chilling Effect of SFFA v. UNC/Harvard on Race-Based Affirmation by Tax-Exempt Charities
91cd3b3295:ab26e9eb371960ca.author: David A. Brennen
91cd3b3295:ab26e9eb371960ca.summary: Recently, the Supreme Court decided in SFFA v. Harvard/UNC that colleges are restricted in their use of race-based affirmative action in admissions. Post- SFFA , many have incorrectly suggested that this means that race may never be considered in admissions. This Article asserts that this expansive view of SFFA is incorrect and leads to a chilling effect on affirmative action by colleges. However, instead of simply asserting that SFFA permits some considerations of race in admissions, the Article goes further by arguing that SFFA does not even apply to admissions by some private colleges. For instance, private colleges that are recipients of federal financial assistance(FFA) must abide by SFFA because of Title VI, which is essentially synonymous with the Equal Protection Clause. But what if a private tax-exempt actor decided to forgo FFA? Could such private actor then lawfully use race-based affirmation action in light of SFFA ? The Article concludes that, even after SFFA , colleges may continue to consider race in admissions to a limited extent. Further, private tax-exempt charities that don’t receive FFA are not subject to SFFA ’s restrictions. Thus, private charities may use race-based affirmative action in admissions—even if such use goes beyond what’s permitted by SFFA .
